panels.text:
Turing's genius was not in building something complex. It was in stripping computation down to its absolute essence.

He asked himself: when a human mathematician sits down to solve a problem, what are they actually doing? They're looking at symbols on paper. They're following rules. They're writing new symbols. They're deciding what to do next based on what they see.

panels.prompt: A young man with dark wavy hair in his twenties sits at a plain wooden desk in a sparse Cambridge study, chin resting on one hand in deep thought, a few sheets of paper before him with diagrams of tape and squares, a pencil in his other hand, soft golden afternoon light through a leaded window illuminates his focused expression, the feeling of an idea forming, contemplative and intimate atmosphere, warm editorial illustration with ink lines and watercolor washes in warm earth tones

panels.text: So Turing imagined the simplest possible version of this process. He called it an a-machine (automatic machine) — we now call it a Turing Machine, a name that came into use after Alonzo Church used it in his 1937 review of Turing's paper — and it has just three parts:

panels.caption: A Turing Machine: tape, head, state register, and rule table

panels.text:
1. An infinite tape divided into cells. Each cell holds a single symbol — a 0, a 1, or blank. The tape stretches infinitely in both directions. This is the machine's memory.

2. A read/write head that sits over one cell at a time. It reads the symbol, can erase it or write a new one, then moves one cell left or right.

3. A rule table — the machine's "brain." A finite list of instructions: "If you're in this state and see this symbol, write this, move this direction, switch to this state."
That's the whole machine. Tape. Head. Rules. State. Nothing else.

panels.text: Imagine a very patient person sitting at an endlessly long scroll of paper, with a pencil, an eraser, and a very precise instruction booklet. They can only see one square at a time. They follow the booklet exactly. No creativity, no shortcuts. Just rules.
Okay, that's the machine in theory. But does it actually DO anything useful? Let's watch one work — step by step.
